title: Serialization and Deserialization
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of serialization and deserialization.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: Serialization converts in-memory data into a representation that can be stored or transmitted; deserialization reconstructs data from that representation. JSON is one possible format. Conversion can lose or alter information: language-specific values may not map cleanly, and serialized data should be treated as untrusted when received. Validate reconstructed data before using it.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs need to convert data between runtime memory and formats that files or other systems can exchange.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
Serialization converts in-memory data into a representation that can be stored or transmitted; deserialization reconstructs data from that representation. JSON is one possible format. Conversion can lose or alter information: language-specific values may not map cleanly, and serialized data should be treated as untrusted when received. Validate reconstructed data before using it.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

examples.title: Serialize an object
examples.explanation: Serialization converts the object to JSON text.

examples.title: Serialize an array
examples.explanation: Arrays can be represented as JSON arrays.

examples.title: Validate after parsing
examples.explanation: Parsing succeeds, but the application may require a numeric count.

examples.title: Consider unsupported values
examples.explanation: Some runtime values may be omitted or transformed during serialization.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Serialize a fictional settings object with a boolean, number, array, and nested object. Deserialize it, then write validation checks for each expected field type.
steps: Serialize a fictional settings object with a boolean, number, array, and nested object. Deserialize it, then write validation checks for each expected field type.
Sketch the communication sequence and identify the client/server roles.
Define expected success and failure outcomes.
Choose checks, timeout or retry behavior where appropriate.
Review your design for privacy and safe handling.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Design a data round-trip exercise. Document the original runtime data, serialized text, reconstructed data, and any value that might be transformed or lost. Include validation for malformed and unexpected data.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy service; do not include live secrets.
